name: Cervicogenic Headache
preview_text: In TCM, a cervicogenic headache is never just a neck problem - it's a signal from the Liver, the Gallbladder, or even an external Cold invasion. Most patients experience a noticeab...
conventional_description:
Cervicogenic headache is a secondary headache disorder, meaning the pain originates not in the head itself but from a problem in the cervical spine or the soft tissues of the neck. The pain is typically one-sided, starts at the base of the skull, and can radiate to the forehead, temple, or behind the eye. It is often accompanied by reduced neck range of motion and tenderness in the upper neck.
Diagnosis is based on clinical signs - such as pain triggered by neck movement or pressure on tender points - and may be confirmed with imaging or diagnostic nerve blocks. Unlike migraines or tension headaches, cervicogenic headache is directly linked to a structural or functional issue in the neck.
conventional_treatments: Conventional management usually begins with physical therapy, manual therapy, and exercises to improve neck posture and strength. Pain-relief medications like NSAIDs are common, and some patients benefit from nerve blocks or trigger point injections. For persistent cases, radiofrequency neurotomy (a procedure that disables pain-carrying nerves) may be considered. While these approaches help many, they primarily target the local neck structures and may not address underlying constitutional factors that make a person prone to recurrence.
tcm_understanding:
TCM sees cervicogenic headache as a disturbance in the flow of Qi and blood through the channels that run along the back and sides of the neck and head. The Gallbladder, Bladder, and Triple Burner channels all pass through this region, and when their smooth movement is obstructed, pain and stiffness result. The obstruction can come from inside - like rising Liver Yang - or from outside, such as an invasion of Wind and Cold.
The location and quality of the pain are key clues. A throbbing, distending headache that starts in the neck and moves to the temples often points to Liver Yang Rising, where internal heat and pressure surge upward. A one-sided, distending pain with neck stiffness and a bitter taste suggests a Lesser Yang stage pattern - a pathogen lodged in the Gallbladder channel.
When the pain is severe, occipital, and triggered by cold exposure, it is usually a Greater Yang Attack of Cold, where external Cold constricts the Bladder channel. A chronic vertex headache with dizziness and cold hands and feet indicates a deeper Terminal Yin stage, where heat and cold have separated in the body.
Because each pattern has a different root, the same diagnosis of cervicogenic headache can require completely different treatments. This is why tongue and pulse examination are essential - they reveal the pattern that the pain alone cannot. A practitioner will look for a red tongue with little coating and a wiry pulse in Liver Yang Rising, or a thin white coat and a floating tight pulse in a Cold invasion.
classical_quote: 「太阳之为病，脉浮，头项强痛而恶寒。」
classical_translation: "In Taiyang disease, the pulse is floating, there is headache and stiff neck, and aversion to cold."

tcm_diagnosis:
A practitioner differentiates patterns by the location and quality of the headache, along with tongue and pulse signs. For throbbing, pounding pain with dizziness and red eyes, Liver Yang Rising is likely. The tongue appears red with little coating, and the pulse is wiry and rapid.
If the pain is a one‑sided distending sensation with neck stiffness, the Lesser Yang stage is suspected. The tongue coat is thin and white, and the pulse feels floating and tight, indicating a pathogen lodged in the channel.
A severe, stiff occipital headache that worsens with cold, often after wind exposure, points to Greater Yang Attack of Cold. The tongue is pale with a thin white coat, and the pulse is floating and tight.
When the headache is chronic, located at the vertex, and accompanied by dizziness and a pale complexion, it suggests a deeper Terminal Yin stage. The tongue may appear red at the tip with a white slippery coat, and the pulse is deep, thin, or wiry.

patterns.symptoms: ["Throbbing or distending pain", "Pain in temples or top of head", "Dizziness or vertigo", "Irritability and quick temper", "Flushed face and red eyes", "Neck stiffness and tension", "Worse with stress and anger"]
patterns.worse_with: Stress and anger, Alcohol and spicy food, Overwork and lack of sleep, Hot, stuffy environments
patterns.better_with: Rest in a dark, quiet room, Cool compress on the forehead, Gentle neck stretches, Deep, slow breathing
patterns.why_this_happens: The Liver keeps Qi and blood flowing smoothly. When emotional stress, frustration, or overwork build up, Liver Yang can surge upward, carrying heat and pressure to the head. This creates a throbbing, distending headache that often begins in the neck as the Gallbladder and Bladder channels tighten, then radiates to the temples or top of the head.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, redder at the sides, with a thin dry yellow or scanty coating. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián), possibly fine (细 xì) and rapid (数 shuò).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Stress and anger directly fan Liver Yang, causing it to surge upward into the head and neck. Alcohol and spicy foods add Heat, making the Yang even more unruly. Overwork and poor sleep deplete the Yin that normally anchors Yang. Rest, calm, and cooling methods help settle the rising Yang, while gentle stretching releases the tight channels in the neck, allowing Qi to flow downward again.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat plenty of cooling, Yin-nourishing foods like cucumber, celery, pear, and spinach. Avoid alcohol, coffee, spicy dishes, and fried food, which add heat and stir up Yang. A regular wind-down routine before bed and gentle daily movement such as tai chi or walking help keep Qi flowing smoothly. Manage stress with deep breathing and avoid bottling up anger.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Lesser Yang stage is a half-exterior, half-interior pattern where a pathogen lodges in the Gallbladder and Triple Burner channels. These channels run along the sides of the head, neck, and shoulders. When the flow of Qi gets stuck, it creates a distending, one-sided headache and a stiff, uncomfortable neck. The struggle between the body's upright Qi and the pathogen can also cause alternating chills and a low-grade fever, while the stuck Qi disrupts the Stomach, making you feel nauseous and leaving a bitter taste in your mouth.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly red body, possible red sides, with a thin white or thin yellow coating. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián) and fine (细 xì), like a taut guitar string that feels slender.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold and wind can penetrate the Lesser Yang channels and trap the pathogen, making the neck stiff and the pain worse. Stress and anger stir up Liver Qi, which feeds directly into the Gallbladder channel, intensifying the distending headache and irritability. Warmth and gentle movement help unblock the stuck Qi, allowing it to flow smoothly again, while simple, warm foods support the Stomach and prevent further stagnation.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, simple meals like congee and steamed vegetables; avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods that can further obstruct Qi. A warm ginger and scallion tea can help the pathogen move out. Keep the neck gently mobile with slow stretches, and avoid sitting in one position for hours. Emotional frustration feeds this pattern, so short breaks and calm breathing make a real difference.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Greater Yang (Taiyang) channels run along the back of the neck and head, forming the body's outermost shield. When external Cold invades these channels, it constricts the flow of Qi and blood, causing the severe, aching pain and rigid stiffness in the occipital region that defines cervicogenic headache.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal body, thin white moist coating. Pulse: floating and tight (浮紧 fú jǐn).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold and wind are the pathogens that invade the Taiyang channels and cause this pattern, so any exposure worsens the constriction and pain. Warmth, rest, and warming herbs like ginger and scallion help the body's defensive Qi push the pathogen back out through the surface, relaxing the tight channels and easing the headache.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep your neck and shoulders warmly covered, especially in windy or cold weather. Sip hot ginger and scallion tea to help your body push the Cold out. Avoid cold drinks, raw foods, and drafts until the acute phase passes.

patterns.why_this_happens: In the Terminal Yin stage, the body's yin and yang have separated, with cold sinking deep into the lower body and heat rising to the head. This creates a unique headache: the cold obstructs the channels in the neck, causing stiffness, while the trapped heat surges upward to the vertex, producing a dull, dizzying pain with a sensation of pressure. The icy hands and feet, combined with a burning chest, reflect this split, and the deep cold weakens the blood and qi, leaving you pale and exhausted.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with a white slippery coat, often redder at the tip. Pulse: wiry, fine or faint.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: In the Terminal Yin stage, yang is already weak and cold has settled deep into the body. Cold exposure worsens that internal cold, making the neck and head pain worse. Emotional stress stirs up Liver qi, which pushes the trapped heat further upward, intensifying the headache and irritability. Warmth, rest, and warm foods help the yang recover and gently counteract the cold. Gentle movement keeps qi moving without burning up your remaining energy, and calming the mind prevents the Liver from flaring, which is key because the Liver channel is the root of this pattern.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups, stews, and congees to support your yang. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that can worsen the internal cold. Keep your neck warm with a scarf, especially in windy or air-conditioned spaces. Gentle daily movement like walking or slow neck stretches helps keep qi flowing without overstraining, and managing stress through deep breathing or meditation can prevent the Liver qi from flaring upward.

faqs.question: How does acupuncture help cervicogenic headaches?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture works by unblocking the channels that run through the neck and head, restoring the smooth flow of Qi and blood. Points like Fengchi GB-20, Tianzhu BL-10, and local tender points are used to release muscle tension and calm the nerves. Depending on your pattern, the acupuncturist may also use points on the hands, feet, or legs to address the root imbalance - for example, Taichong LR-3 to subdue Liver Yang or Waiguan SJ-5 to harmonize the Lesser Yang channel. Many patients feel immediate relief after a session, but lasting change usually requires a course of treatment.

faqs.question: Can I use TCM alongside my current pain medications or nerve blocks?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM can safely complement most conventional treatments. Acupuncture and herbal formulas are often used together with physical therapy or medications. However, certain herbs - such as Chuan Xiong (Ligusticum) or Dang Gui (Angelica sinensis) - have mild blood-moving effects and may interact with anticoagulant or antiplatelet drugs. Always bring a full list of your medications to your TCM practitioner and inform your doctor that you are receiving TCM. Do not stop prescribed treatments abruptly without medical guidance.

faqs.question: What if my headache is caused by a disc problem or arthritis?
faqs.answer: TCM does not ignore structural issues. While the underlying pattern is treated with herbs and acupuncture, local points around the neck can help relax muscles, reduce inflammation, and improve mobility. Many people with degenerative changes or disc problems find that TCM reduces the frequency and intensity of their headaches by addressing the energetic imbalance that makes the neck vulnerable. It is not a replacement for necessary orthopedic care, but it can be a powerful complement.

faqs.question: How many acupuncture sessions will I need?
faqs.answer: A typical course is one to two sessions per week for four to eight weeks, but this varies by pattern. Acute Cold invasions may resolve in just a few visits, while chronic Liver Yang Rising or Terminal Yin patterns often need longer. Your practitioner will reassess your progress regularly and adjust the frequency. Many patients continue with monthly maintenance sessions after the main course to prevent recurrence.

faqs.question: Will the herbs have side effects?
faqs.answer: When prescribed by a qualified practitioner, Chinese herbal formulas are generally well tolerated. Side effects are rare and usually mild - such as slight digestive changes - and can be managed by adjusting the formula. Because formulas are tailored to your specific pattern, they avoid the one-size-fits-all approach. Be sure to inform your practitioner of any known allergies or sensitivities.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe during pregnancy if I have cervicogenic headaches?
faqs.answer: Many acupuncture points and herbs are safe during pregnancy, but some must be avoided because they can stimulate the uterus or affect hormone levels. Always inform your practitioner if you are pregnant or trying to conceive. A skilled TCM provider will select points and herbs that are safe for both you and your baby, and they may focus more on gentle acupuncture and dietary therapy rather than strong herbal decoctions.

faqs.question: Do I need to change my diet to get better?
faqs.answer: Diet plays a supportive role. In general, it is best to avoid cold and raw foods that can obstruct Qi, especially if your headache is triggered by cold or dampness. If your pattern involves Liver Yang Rising, steer clear of spicy, greasy, or fried foods that stir up heat. Warm, cooked meals, ginger tea, and foods that nourish the Liver - like black sesame or goji berries - are often recommended. Your practitioner will give you specific guidance based on your pattern.

research.title: Clinical Application Characteristics of Acupuncture for Cervicogenic Headache: A Complex Network Analysis
research.description: This study used complex network analysis to identify the most frequently used acupoints and treatment patterns for cervicogenic headache in Chinese clinical practice. The core acupoint combination was Fengchi (GB20), Baihui (DU20), Tianzhu (BL10), and cervical Jiaji points. The primary treatment principles were dispelling wind, dredging the channels, and calming the Liver to suppress Yang.
research.periodical: Authors not specified. Clinical Application Characteristics of Acupuncture for Cervicogenic Headache Based on Complex Network Analysis. Journal of Acupuncture and Tuina Science, 2024.

research.title: Observation on the Therapeutic Effect of Different Acupuncture Postures for Cervicogenic Headache
research.description: This clinical trial compared the efficacy of acupuncture administered in a sitting position versus a supine position for patients with cervicogenic headache. Both postures significantly reduced pain, but the sitting position showed a slight advantage in relieving neck stiffness and improving cervical range of motion.
research.periodical: Authors not specified. Observation on the Therapeutic Effect of Different Acupuncture Postures for Cervicogenic Headache. Acupuncture Research, 2023.
